#1978. Cristiano Ronaldo tribute party hilariously ruined with help of Newcastle United star

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

The Cristiano Ronaldo tribute party hilariously ended in disaster.

The Estádio Municipal de Braga hosting what was intended to be a celebration of the selfish prima donna’s international career.

It had always been about Cristiano Ronaldo rather than the team.

The 41-year-old embarrassingly walked out of the Portugal camp in September after he was told he would not start the in the Nations League away match against Denmark.

Cristiano Ronaldo was given a token £215 fine and 30-day suspension by Portugal.

Fast forward less than two months later and ahead of the reverse fixture with Denmark, he was at it again.

Rather than doing things properly, Cristiano Ronaldo retired from international football via a video he posted on his social media last week. No advance warning given and Portugal coach Jorge Jesus later revealed that Ronaldo would have been picked for these Uefa Nations League games against Denmark and Wales in November.

With his out of the blue announcement, Portugal then quickly made this Saturday night Portugal v Denmark match all about Cristiano Ronaldo.

All of the Portugal players and the mascots walked out wearing a ‘Ronaldo 7’ shirt.

The fans displayed the word ‘Ronaldo’ in the top tier of one of the stands.

A banner that translated as ‘thank you, captain’, plus a similar message appearing on the scoreboard in the seventh minute.

How brilliant it was then that this all ended in disaster.

Pierre-Emile Hojbjerg scored a penalty just before half-time, then Rasmus Hojlund scored twice in eight minutes to make it 3-0 with more than half an hour remaining.

With 73 minutes on the clock Newcastle United striker William Osula came off the bench and within a minute had won a free-kick towards the right wing. The resultant free-kick seeing Joachim Andersen head the fourth and the Cristano Ronaldo fan club left in tears as his tribute well and truly had fallen apart.

Osula came close to adding a fifth but unlucky to see his late effort blocked.

Bernardo Silva did get a no consolation goal for Portugal in the third minute of added time but the final 4-1 humiliating scoreline at home, was such a fitting tribute to Cristiano Ronaldo.

#1977. Liberali praises Cisse and looks back on Milan decision: “It wasn’t easy”

Mattia Liberali has looked back on his decision to leave AC Milan and to snub rejoining them, insisting he has ‘no regrets’.

After making his way through the youth sector, Liberali burst onto the scene in the 2024 summer preseason under Paulo Fonseca. He also made his first senior start under the Portuguese coach, but then found chances hard to come by and opted to leave the following year.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

On Tuesday afternoon, Liberali spoke in the press conference room at Coverciano – the Italian national team headquarters – alongside Alphadjo Cisse. The pair were team-mates at Catanzaro last season and could have reunite at Milan, but the former chose to head to Cesc Fabregas’ Como.

Speaking to the reporters present, Liberali once again commented on why he wanted to leave Milan in the first place to head to the Serie B side. His words were relayed by MilanNews.

Is there any regret about how things ended with Milan?

“No regrets. You have to make decisions with confidence and not look back. I’m very happy for Cisse, who’s succeeding. It wasn’t easy leaving AC Milan, but it’s always important to look forward.”

What was it like making the jump to Como?

“It’s not easy to go from Serie B to the intensity of Serie A and the Champions League. Aquilani? I’m sorry about his dismissal, he helped me so much last year. I’ll write to him in the next few days, I’m sorry he wasn’t able to make his mark at Sassuolo.”

#1976. A message for Newcastle United fans ‘Please positively support the team’

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

A message for my fellow Newcastle United fans.

There is a sound in sport more discordant than the pure roar of opposition.

Our recent Everton home match showcased it.

It was loud, and it was often, and it was heard by football fans all around the world. It is the sound of a home crowd turning on its own. At St. James’ Park, that sound has been heard with increasing frequency in recent matches—sharp, collective, and unmistakable.

Newcastle United fans, among the most passionate and historically loyal in English football, have at times directed their frustration not solely at the referee or the visiting side, but at the men in black and white who wear the shirt they revere. And while discontent is a fan’s prerogative, the practice of booing one’s own players carries consequences that extend far beyond a single afternoon’s dissatisfaction. It damages the athletes who must perform under it’s weight and it slowly erodes the very reputation of the supporters who claim to love the club most.

Consider first the players. Professional footballers are not automata. They are human beings operating at the outer edge of physical and psychological demand, often carrying the accumulated pressure of ownership expectations, media scrutiny, and the weight of a city’s hopes. When the crowd that once lifted them now turns its voice against them, the effect is not motivational theatre. It is corrosive.

Confidence is a fragile commodity in sport; once fractured in public, it is slow to mend. A player (especially a young or new player) who hears the boos after a misplaced pass or a missed chance does not suddenly discover a higher gear. More often he tightens, second-guesses, and retreats into the safety of safer choices. The game becomes smaller. Risk—the very quality that produces moments of brilliance—becomes something to be avoided.

History offers quiet lessons. The great teams of the past were not immune to periods of struggle, yet the bond between player and supporter was understood as reciprocal. Kevin Keegan’s side of the mid-1990s rode waves of belief that were almost tangible. Even in disappointment, the underlying current remained one of shared purpose.

When that current reverses, the club’s identity begins to fray. Players notice. They speak of it privately, if not always publicly. They adjust their body language, their willingness to demand the ball, their instinct to press high. What the stands intend as accountability can register on the pitch as abandonment. For those of us that have played footy at any level (or any public activity) – loud criticism seldom inspires, it creates a heavier load.

There is also the matter of reputation—the intangible but real currency of a club’s supporters. Newcastle United fans have long been celebrated for their loyalty through lean decades, for the sheer volume and colour they bring to the occasion, for the sense that the club and the city are inseparable. That reputation is not automatic. It is earned, season after season, through constancy of support that does not evaporate when results turn. Booing one’s own players, particularly in sustained fashion, risks rewriting that narrative. Outside observers—pundits, rival supporters, potential recruits—begin to form a different picture: of a crowd that is quick to turn, of an atmosphere that can become hostile even to those fighting in the same colours. Perception hardens. The next talented midfielder weighing a move, the young academy graduate deciding whether to commit his future, the manager assessing the environment he would inherit—all of them factor atmosphere into the equation. A club that once marketed itself on the passion of its people can find that passion reinterpreted as volatility.

None of this is an argument for silence or passive acceptance of mediocrity. Criticism is legitimate. I would argue, and I believe that most would agree, a team of players can inspire the crowd but that the reverse is true also. A crowd can create positive energy that propels the team on the pitch. It is a symbiotic relationship – and its this relationship that can make the home field a fortress. A negative reaction from the crowd can also beget poorer play on the pitch. Yes, boards, managers, and players should be held to account. But there is a distinction between demanding better and actively undermining those currently charged with delivering it. The former can be expressed through measured reaction, through pointed but constructive noise after the final whistle, through the continued presence and volume that still says “this matters.” The latter—booing in real time—sends a different message: that the relationship is conditional, and that the players are no longer considered part of the collective struggle. And when coming from the Gallowgate, arguably the most passionate fans anywhere, their negativity sets the tone for all.

Sport at its best creates a temporary community in which strangers become, for ninety minutes, something closer to allies. That community is tested when results fail. How it responds in those moments reveals its character. Newcastle United fans have, through far darker periods than the present, demonstrated a capacity for loyalty that borders on the heroic. The question now is whether that tradition will be preserved when the going is merely difficult rather than desperate. The players will answer on the pitch. The reputation of the fans will be answered in the stands—by the choice of what sound they choose to make when the team needs them most.

I know the players make a lot of money. I also know that buying the ticket gives each fan the right to express themselves in their own way. But, actions have consequences, and, in my opinion, booing your own players is like “keeping up the whippings until morale improves.” 🎙️ THE MAG PODCAST Ep 15: Fulham frustration, Newcastle United’s season report card and Relegation fears Listen to the latest episode of The Mag Pod! #1975. “Nightmare outing” | West Ham lynchpin gets hammered in “confidence draining” 90 minutes

Two days ago it was Tomas Soucek who suffered the ignominy of a late error costing his side a goal and the game as Spain ran out 2 – 0 winners against his Czech Republic.

Last night it was his West Ham team mate Dinos Mavropanos who endured a horror 90 minutes up against former team mate Crysencio Summerville’s Netherlands, in which the Dutch team racked up a 7-0 destruction job of Dinos’ Greece.

Understandably, West Ham’s lynchpin centre back didn’t emerge from the mauling with anything other than widespread criticism. Sportsdunia.com didn’t mix their words when it came to rating Dinos’ performance the as poorest of the eleven:

Konstantinos Mavropanos – 3.5: This was a nightmare outing, and you could almost see his confidence draining. He conceded corners early and never truly recovered positionally against the Dutch interchanges. The big missed header at 30 minutes summed up his evening, a rare attacking contribution wasted.

7 – 0 drubbing would have been a real confidence – draining result, with another game just around the corner

The error that led to a goal reflected poor concentration more than lack of ability. From our perspective, he looked overwhelmed by the movement of Reijnders and Malen.”

After remaining unbeaten through their four internationals in September, this will have been a shattering blow to the Greece side’s confidence. They’ll have only 3 days to pick themselves up before a home tie on Monday night against Serbia, Mavropanos’ side still sitting second in the group thanks to that purple patch in September but no doubt reeling from their schooling last night.

West Ham fans will be hoping that Mavropanos can be part of a confidence – building resurrection by the national side next week so that he at least returns to east London in a slightly better frame of mind than he must be in just now.

#1974. Premier League KMI panel issues emphatic verdict on Alexander Isak penalty decision v Arsenal

The Premier League’s Key Match Incidents (KMI) Panel has concluded that Liverpool should’ve had a penalty awarded for an offence by Jurrien Timber on Alexander Isak in their defeat to Arsenal earlier this month.

Five minutes after Kai Havertz scored the only goal of the game at Anfield, the Swedish striker had his shirt pulled in the box by the Gunners defender, but neither on-field referee Andy Madley nor Stuart Attwell on VAR felt compelled to award a spot kick despite the transgression being clear.

The Reds’ head coach Andoni Iraola went as far as claiming that a penalty would’ve been awarded had our number 9 gone to ground instead of staying on his feet when his jersey was grabbed.

On Wednesday, the Premier League published the findings of several incidents reviewed by the KMI Panel, including the one involving Isak and Timber on 1 November.

Their verdict reads (via premierleague.com): ‘The panel felt that a penalty should have been awarded for a holding action by Timber on Isak, 4:1. One panellist considered the short-lived holding to lack clear impact on the ability of Isak to progress.

‘The majority also felt that VAR should have intervened to recommend an on-field review, 3:2, on the basis that it was a clear and obvious error. Two panellists considered that the subjectivity in assessing impact meant this did not meet the high threshold for VAR intervention.’

The KMI Panel concluded: ‘In this instance the panel deemed that Timber’s challenge on Isak met the threshold for a holding offence and should have resulted in a penalty kick, both on-field and through VAR intervention.’

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

How nice of the KMI Panel to come back and tell us what was so damn obvious at the time of the incident – or at least obvious to anyone not named Andy Madley or Stuart Attwell, or whichever member of the panel felt that the right decision was made on the day.

How that individual concluded that Timber’s actions lacked ‘clear impact on the ability of Isak to progress’ is baffling – the Liverpool striker would surely have gotten on the end of Bradley Barcola’s cross had his shirt not been so blatantly pulled.

The panel’s verdict today won’t come as much consolation to anyone involved with the Reds, who were deprived of a legitimate penalty which – if converted – could’ve significantly altered the course of a match that they lost 1-0.

It’s not much good being told in retrospect that the officials got it wrong; these are clear decisions that professional referees should be capable of getting correct at the time, especially when they have the fallback option of VAR.

We get that many incidents are subjective and that consensus will never be achieved when it comes to refereeing in the Premier League, but there’s simply no excuse for botching calls like the Timber/Isak incident 10 days ago.

With key players absent on international duty, these mid-international break training sessions are challenging for coaching staff who are keen to improve the team but of course don’t get to drill the whole squad.

West Ham United, though, with their reduced circumstances this season, have fewer players away than in the ‘old days’ of the Premier League thanks to player departures and others – like skipper Jarrod Bowen – simply being overlooked by their national coaches.

Yesterdays ‘inside training’ video shows clear blue water between the old days of Nuno Espírito Santo and the new-era Scott Parker training session. The very public participation of former ‘discards’ Edson Alvarez and Soungoutou Magassa – both featured from the outset along with perennial discard Maxi Cornet – shows Parker’s pledge to wipe the slate clean has being carried out.

Integrated and back in full training along with Edson Alvarez: Soungoutou Magassa

#1971. ‘Not ready’, ‘out of control’ and ‘the end of the world’: What Amorim’s words tell us about Milan’s state

Ruben Amorim is not one to hold back when it comes to speaking his thoughts to the media, and the last few days are no exception.

The past week or so has seen Amorim have to digest the best and worst of his AC Milan side. The 3-1 derby win over Inter generated a euphoria that begun whispers of the word ‘Scudetto’, before a dismal defeat to Ferencvaros which saw Milan drop to 29th in the Europa League standings.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

This rollercoaster of extremes didn’t stop either side of those two games either. Before the victory over the Nerazzurri a 2-1 lead had been coughed up against Bologna, who scored three times in the second half to win at San Siro and inflict the first league defeat on the Rossoneri.

Yesterday, the Diavolo responded to the season low-point against the Hungarians by beating a Genoa side that had won their last three games and four of their last five. This Milan team is a very difficult one to work out, and it seems even the manager is struggling to do so.

After the Ferencvaros and Genoa games, we learned a lot about where Amorim sees his team to be at. Some key lines from his post-match comments demonstrated a wide spectrum of reaction, from anger to pride, passing through encouragement and worry.

Ruben Amorim has often gone to bat for his players after negative performances and results this season, but it seems that the defeat on Thursday night had pushed his patience to the brink as he tore into his team after the game.

“There’s no explanation. There’s nothing I can say, especially about the first half. I don’t remember another first half like it. It’s about ambition, concentration, desire,” he said.

“We gave away opportunities, we gave away stupid gifts. We weren’t prepared to play football tonight. I usually have a lot to say in defence of our team, but not tonight. We need to be more humble and understand what happened.”

For the first time we saw a peek behind the mask, one that has very often been one portraying an optimistic and positive expression. Amorim knew there was no point attempting to lie to the supporters, the media but above all to himself.

What we know is that Amorim echoed the ferocity of these sentiments when speaking in the dressing room after full-time in what was likely the first dressing down that the team got. Six players were reported to have disappointed more than the others, too.

Above all, what stood out was the fact that the head coach opted to question whether his players wanted it enough. This was no longer a question of learning an identity, rotation or an injury crisis: it became a matter of heart.

Another intriguing extract from the post-Ferencvaros tirade that Amorim went on was about the squad’s ability to balance playing in two different competitions, namely Serie A and the Europa League.

“We’re not ready to be competitive on two fronts. We need to work on our way of looking at football and how we approach matches. There are no excuses tonight, there’s nothing I can say.

“I have to focus on the league, obviously, but we also have to do well in the Europa League. We must and can win games despite the rotation. We have to be ready – we’re not now – to play and win every three days.

“But I won’t give up on this competition. But as long as the mathematics don’t condemn us, we’ll fight in this competition as we do in the others.”

Once again, Amorim offered a bit of a revelation: the league is the absolute priority for Milan this season. It may not exactly be revolutionary information, given that a top four spot remains the most accessible avenue to the main objective for 2026-27: securing a Champions League return.

And yet, in his emotional outburst, the former Sporting CP and Manchester United boss told us all in black and white that Serie A will be the focus. As a result, it’s right to expect more ups and downs in Europe, especially with such a depleted squad.

There is an element of observational realism about Amorim’s words; almost an admission of defeat in his attempts to spin two plates at the same time and get the most out of the resources at his disposal. Does it suggest a Europa League resurgence is coming? Not exactly.

Amorim has not made a habit of mentioning individuals ever since his arrivals, both in his pre-match words but especially after games in which emotions are running high. However, he brought up someone who was absent for the Ferencvaros game.

“Everyone needs to train like Pavlovic. He’s ready to die in training. He’s a good example. Sometimes when players don’t start, they struggle. But there are no excuses, we should have won even with those who started,” he said.

Going into the season there were some who were legitimately questioning whether Strahinja Pavlovic would even be a tactical fit for Amorim’s usual 3-4-2-1 system, given that he prefers more composed, ball-playing outside centre-backs.

The answer to those doubts is that in November the Serbian has become the shining light in the eyes of his manager. We mentioned earlier that it had become a question of heart, and nobody can doubt that Pavlovic has that in abundance.

For all of the talk about tactics, systems, shapes and patterns, football is a simple game that very often comes down to who wants it more. In this regard, Amorim elevated Pavlovic as the example to follow, while hoping he returns from injury for the Frosinone game after the break.

Moving on to the post-Genoa reflections, what was quite apparent was that Ruben Amorim was in no mood to get carried away. In fact, if anything, he revealed his belief that his team are still miles off where he wants them.

“What I feel is that, when we’re competitive, we’re difficult to beat, and now we’re steering the game towards our style. We push for control with the ball.

“When we’re not able to be competitive, we’re completely out of control. It’s a big difference, but it’s something we need to work on. But again, the team’s evolution, the way we’re playing, is completely different from the start of the season, and I’m happy with that.

“We should have more points. I’m clearly not happy with the European games, not just because of the results, but because of the performance. Results can happen, but the performances are far from what we want. However, I think we’ll be a better team in the future.”

So, for now this version of Milan is not one that satisfies the coach. The words are a good summary of what the last six games have shown, in which there have been an even split of victories and defeats: on their day the team can beat anyone in the league, but on an off-day they can lose to anyone too.

What Amorim seems keen to hammer home is that progress for this season will be judged on the ability to bring the ceiling closer to the floor. In other words, we have seen the potential of this team already with some impressive wins, yet the base level for performances remains frighteningly low.

Consistency is not just about being able to string together several positive results in a row, something the current Rossoneri do not seem capable of. It is about the repeated displaying of an idea and an identity every few days, to suggest the team are getting closer to the vision the coach has.

Various things make that difficult (perhaps unachievable, based on Amorim’s other comments) right now, such as the injury situation and the multiple windows needed to sculpt the squad. Progress is not always linear, but the target has been set.

One of the themes that Amorim has been consistently questioned on this season is how to unlock the club-record signing Goncalo Ramos, who remains stuck on three goals (one of which was a penalty).

After the Genoa game, he said: “I think we’re lacking time in the final third. We control the ball away from the opponent’s penalty area. This is also key for Goncalo Ramos to have more clear-cut chances. It’s clearly not Goncalo’s fault.

“Pulisic is far from the penalty area. Gonçalo is far from the penalty area. All these players play away from the penalty area, so I can say we’re still far from the final product, because we’re still working on good progression, but then in the final third of the pitch we waste a lot of time with the ball there.”

This is one of the points of ‘evolution’ that Amorim clearly wants to see from his side, but is yet to achieve. Milan are not yet a team that can sustain pressure in the opposition half, nor can they penetrate the box with any regularity either.

In fact, a report from Sky backed this up with some interesting numbers, look specifically at data per 30 minutes of actual possession. Milan are first in Serie A for build-up actions, but they are 20th for entries into the final third and entries into the opposition box.

Amorim’s side are 19th for percentage of touches in the attacking third and 18th in percentage of touches in the opposition box. When the Rossoneri have the ball, it is rarely in a threatening area.

With numbers like these, there isn’t much for Ramos to get on the end of, and it makes the positive attacking numbers (23 goals in 11 league games) feel quite unsustainable.

The Portuguese striker meanwhile is first in the Milan squad in Serie A for interceptions, recoveries, touches in the middle third and touches in the opposition half. He is second for receptions, touches and duels, and third for passes.

Simply put, the No.9 is being drawn away from the area he should be operating in because the team are not capable of sustaining spells of possession further up the field, so he needs to drop deeper to feel involved.

This is something Amorim must work on, because while the goals are coming from other sources for now – in some cases due to the space Ramos helps create – it could all come tumbling down unless the attacking play improves more generally.

🚨🎙️🛡️ Ruben Amorim on Gonçalo Ramos: “Ramos is helping US more than we are helping him. It’s a TEAM problem, not a Ramos problem.”

“We don’t spend enough time in the final third.”

“When we start keeping the ball there more often, Gonçalo is going to score MANY goals.” pic.twitter.com/b3Zs6YxNym

— Milan Wire (@MilanWireX) November 8, 2026

Finally, we end with what was perhaps the most passionate part of Amorim’s comments following the win at the Stadio Luigi Ferraris on Sunday, again centred around the levels he expects from his team.

“It’s the mentality. When you’re a player, there are no off days. If you play for Milan, for these clubs, there are no off days. You can’t show up like we did on Thursday and then turn it on again for Sunday. It’s not possible, it’s not something that will work.

“It’s not a physical condition, it’s a question of anxiety about defeat. If you ‘panic’ about defeat, it’s not that you’re afraid of losing, but that you know that losing is the end of the world. That’s the feeling I want my teams to have.”

In many ways, the manager was speaking in a way that channels how fans have experienced the past week. How is it possible that Milan can be completely outplayed by a side sat third in the Hungarian lead just days after convincingly beating the Italian champions?

Against Genoa, how can the team play as they did in the first half, and then appear to completely drop off a cliff in the second half when the time came to dig deep and bring the result home? The disparity in levels both in-game and from match to match is astounding everyone, even the man in charge.

What Amorim said about wanting his side to fear losing was particularly poignant. In his time at the club so far he has repeatedly stressed that feeling of responsibility to honour the red and black shirt and all that comes with that, including the importance of results.

Some may argue that encouraging an ‘end of the world’ type mentality will not help the players play more carefree and will actually only stiffen them up. Yet, it could also provide the stimulus for the fight and the courage that Amorim clearly so desperately wants.

There is a hint of irony about the ‘no days off’ comment, as Amorim has given the squad a one-week break, at least those who were not called up by their national teams. When everyone reconvenes there will be another crucial stretch of games to see out the year, starting with a home match against the surprise package Frosinone.

For all of the energy, passion and emotion that Ruben Amorim speaks with, it will eventually be time for words to become deeds. Consistency must be not a distant mirage but some thing tangible that emerges.

Only then will a full buy-in be achieved and patience be awarded. Otherwise there will always be the fear that darkness follows light.

“Losing on purpose” sounds great but once you get down on a human level where you understand player perform better when they are in form, playing against a team like Ferencváros should be a confidence booster not a question mark. We have a deeper squad than como spend 20 million more in wages and have the same amount of injuries. Us losing to Ferencváros is not acceptable in my opinion.

In fact Como have 1 less injury than us, playing consistently with the same starting 11. Here we are trying to play chess with potential injuries and end up with more than teams that just play their best 11 and rotate normally the players that needs it.

When you are a one team wonder and got a reality check in England, no actual identity, want to play heavy metal football in seria a, can’t understand your team in months…well what should we expect!!!!!

What is ridicoulous, which part? 😂😂 Amorim being a one team wonder? Not having a set formation and team? Clowns like Coco believing he is the mesiah and will bring Milan back to the top? He wasn’t ever on top, he doesn’t know how. He only tells stories, but results and stats don’t back them up.

I’d love to see you expand on that because I can’t find anything wrong with it. He has a been a one team wonder, he was laughed at in England and he seems to have no idea about his squad even at this point.

Amorim keeps talking about bringing the club back to the top but he has neither the knowledge or the experience to do that. So it will be a nice story to remember when he is fired.

In a way we don’t have enough quality players and lack depth. But… What about Bologna or Ferencváros? Do they have superior rosters? Nope. So the “we don’t have enough good players” claim doesn’t explain everything.

A better coach can get the best out of every player. Just look at e.g. FK Bodø/Glimt. They’ve beaten clubs with far better squads recent years without any great players.

#1970. Chelsea are great entertainers but possess clear weakness

Chelsea are promising to be this season’s Premier League entertainers and yet manager Xabi Alonso seemingly believes less is more when it comes to possession.

Alonso has started with two wins from two league games in charge of Chelsea, with his team scoring seven goals and conceding five. So far, it has been a lot of fun – if not entirely convincing.

But perhaps the most significant numbers are around how much – or how little – Chelsea are having the ball. Having finished their 3-2 victory over Fulham with 38.11 per cent of possession, Chelsea had just 25.6 per cent in the 4-3 success over Brighton and Hove Albion and successfully completed 146 passes. Both were their lowest figures on record in the Premier League.

“The data is not important,” Alonso said. “It’s how you play and what we can do better. I don’t say ‘today we need to have 60 per cent or 20 per cent’. I never talk about those things. It’s about how to prepare, how to be more competitive.”

Chelsea’s third goal against Brighton, scored in the 32nd minute, best summed up the London club under Alonso to date. It took the home side three passes to go from the edge of their own penalty area to João Pedro scoring against his former club.

Jorrel Hato passed the ball to Morgan Rogers, he then released Hato down the left and the wing-back slid the ball across for João Pedro to finish. It was a devastating counter-attack and should have put Chelsea on course for a much easier win.

Joao Pedro finishes off a deadly Chelsea counter-attack and gives the Blues a 3-0 lead 🔥 pic.twitter.com/wAr0ckIgXJ

“After 30 minutes, we are 3-0 and probably, in that moment, we have played too much the result,” Alonso said. “It’s quite normal, it happens in many teams. I am sure in the future we can manage it better.”

It is one thing outscoring Fulham and a depleted Brighton team without having the ball, but can Chelsea do that against the bigger and better teams? We will get an early indicator in the next game against Arsenal at the Emirates.

Alonso’s approach has some similarities to the way in which Antonio Conte set up his Chelsea title-winning team. Just as Conte converted Victor Moses into an effective right wing-back, Alonso started Pedro Neto there on Sunday.

After Roméo Lavia had opened the scoring, it was Neto who grabbed Chelsea’s second goal against Brighton by drifting into the penalty area to finish from Rogers’s low cross.

"It's a nightmare for the goalkeeper!"Bart Verbruggen and Mats Wieffer's collision leads to Romeo Lavia scoring his first goal for Chelsea ⚽️ pic.twitter.com/q5awbdwVV0

"Pedro Neto Pounces!"Morgan Rogers goes past his defender before sliding the ball across to Neto! 💥 pic.twitter.com/WHZCIGsOLl

But whereas Conte’s team gave up little at the back, Alonso’s Chelsea are yet to balance their effective transitional play with shutting out their opponents.

Neto was partly to blame for Brighton’s first goal, as he missed a challenge in the build-up to Malick Yalcouyé’s brilliant volley. Making his Chelsea debut, goalkeeper Emiliano Martínez could do nothing to stop it and can expect to be kept busy this season if things do not change.

“I have come here to challenge and to try and win the Premier League,” Martínez said. “I know the talent we have up front. I try to bring that solidity at the back.”

"Yalcouye with a sumptuous volley!"Malick Yalcouye puts Brighton on the scoreboard with a venomous volley 😳 pic.twitter.com/8UeeyvPjUw

Conte’s Chelsea had N’Golo Kanté to mop up in midfield and that is an area of the pitch that is causing Alonso some difficulties. Manchester City target Enzo Fernández was once again left out of the squad and Moisés Caicedo was not deemed fit enough to start.

Caicedo was eventually thrown on when Chelsea were trying to stop Brighton completing a remarkable comeback, but he was quickly forced off again with an injury. The club have been exploring a move for Monaco midfielder Lamine Camara and that need looks even more pressing now.

“We want the best for the team and that’s why we took a decision [on Fernández] against Luton and today,” Alonso said. “What’s going to develop? We’re not sure. We can prepare. We are preparing for all the scenarios. But I assure you that whatever happens, from Wednesday [when the transfer window is shut] we’ll have a good enough squad to compete in all the Premier League games.”

Chelsea’s new set-piece coach Austin MacPhee had celebrated Lavia’s goal, which came partly as a result of a corner but owed more to a mistake from Brighton goalkeeper Bart Verbruggen.

MacPhee, however, will not have liked Brighton’s second-half goals. It was from a short corner that the visitors managed to work the ball to Pascal Gross and his cross was diverted into his own net by João Pedro.

Joao Pedro puts Pascal Groß's cross into his own net and Brighton have brought it back to 3-2 👀 pic.twitter.com/maBMwVu3DC

Gross’s headed third goal also came at the end of a set-piece, but, fortunately for Chelsea, it was in the sixth minute of added time and Cole Palmer had already made the points safe for the home team before then.

Palmer had done little to impress watching England head coach Thomas Tuchel until he picked up the ball in the 74th minute, shrugged off two Brighton challenges and produced a brilliant finish to beat Verbruggen.

Cole Palmer finishes EXPERTLY to give Chelsea their two-goal cushion back 💥 pic.twitter.com/6xI9W8xe2q

Fabian Hürzeler, the Brighton manager, said his team “dominated” the game, but acknowledged: “I think if you spend so much money on these kinds of players, like Rogers, Palmer or João [Pedro], then, of course, a team like Chelsea can rely on this individual quality. And they showed it in certain moments of the game.”

Palmer, João Pedro and Rogers are clearly going to be a huge problem for Chelsea’s opponents. But Alonso’s team cannot rely on having to score three or four goals to win games. And they might need to have a bit more of the ball.

"The game today was a special game for me." João Pedro says he was happy with his performance for Chelsea against Brighton 🔵 pic.twitter.com/fWSqWo7ert

6 - João Pedro today was the sixth player (and first for Chelsea) to score a goal, assist a goal, and score an own goal in the same Premier League game, and first since Tottenham Hotspur's Son Heung-min against Man City in December 2023.Eventful. pic.twitter.com/xRVjqkOY9D

The final game of the day comes from the north west as Manchester United host newly-promoted Ipswich. That game kicks off at 4.30pm and you can follow all the live action from that match right here.

Chelsea 4 Brighton 3 Leeds 1 Brentford 1 Sunderland 1 Fulham 0

Possession: Chelsea 26%-74% BrightonShots: 17-15Shots on target: 6-6Corners: 4-7Touches in opposition box: 29-28

There is no time for Brighton to push for the equaliser as the final whistle is blown at Stamford Bridge. Chelsea make it two wins from two to start the new Premier League season but were pushed all the way by Brighton. It finishes 4-3 at Stamford Bridge.

It could well be the last touch of the game but Brighton have a small amount of hope as Gross heads past Martinez. If that had come a few minutes ago, maybe Brighton could have pushed for a draw.

Brighton have a corner and if they are to have any chance of potentially rescuing a point, they have to score right now. De Cuyper’s inswinger is clipped into a dangerous area but for some odd reason referee Michael Oliver gives Chelsea a free-kick. Absolutely ridiculous decision; there was no foul in any way, shape or form.

Chelsea look to counter through Pedro, who is then brought down by Costinha. It is an easy booking for referee Michael Oliver to give.

How many added minutes will there be? The answer is five minutes.

Boscagli is booked for bringing down Rogers.

This is a concern for Chelsea as Caicedo, who came on as a second-half substitute, is now having to go off injured. In his place is former Brighton man Barco, who slapped Bellingham at the World Cup. Barco is booed vociferously by the travelling Brighton fans.

Meanwhile Leeds are level 1-1 against Brentford at Elland Road thanks to Calvert-Lewin’s equaliser.

Double change for Brighton as Costinha and David replace Wieffer and Kostoulas.

Brighton scored four a week ago against Aston Villa on the opening weekend but have conceded four this weekend. If they can get a goal though soon, it would make the home fans inside Stamford Bridge very nervous.

Kadioglu has an effort from the edge of the Chelsea box but drags his effort wide.

Meanwhile, up in the north east, Isidor has put Sunderland 1-0 up against Fulham at the Stadium of Light.

Palmer has been pretty quiet today but Chelsea’s two-goal lead is restored. He receives it from Pedro and drives forward through the Brighton half. As he approaches the edge of the penalty area, Palmer calmly slots home into the bottom corner.

Cole Palmer finishes EXPERTLY to give Chelsea their two-goal cushion back 💥 pic.twitter.com/6xI9W8xe2q

Tuchel will have like that. He may not have had a brilliant game, but Palmer just scored a brilliant goal. That should be enough for Chelsea.

Fabian Hurzeler turns to his bench for the first time today as Osman comes on for Yalcouye, who was impressive.

Xabi Alonso turns to his bench again as Chavarria replaces Colwill.

We have this news from the Premier League:

#CHEBHAMatch Officials are operating in the second half without communications packs due to an ongoing technical issue. VAR remains in operation via a back-up system using messages sent to the referee's watch and radio communication to the fourth official if required.

Dunk is in trouble. The ball is played forward by Gusto down the right channel to pick out the run of Pedro into the Brighton half. Dunk brings Pedro down but is fortunate that Vuskovic was covering so that is why there is no red card. Dunk is rightly booked.

Chelsea are on the ropes at the moment and Brighton can sense another goal. Boscagli is the latest Brighton player to have an effort and Martinez is forced into a decent save down to his left.

Xabi Alonso is going to respond to the Brighton momentum with a triple change. James, Acheampong and Caicedo replace Neto, Lavia and Fofana.

It is all Brighton and Chelsea are seriously wobbling. Gomez has his fourth chance of the second half and is not far off scoring as his effort hits the side netting. You can sense the anxiety inside Stamford Bridge and it is the travelling Brighton fans making all the noise.

This game is well and truly back on. Chelsea looked in complete control at 3-0 up but now there is just one goal in it. Brighton work a corner short and appear to have wasted the chance but Yalcouye slides a wonderful pass into the right side of the box to pick out the run of Gross, whose shot/cross takes a big deflection off former Brighton man Pedro and goes past Martinez into the Chelsea net.

Joao Pedro puts Pascal Groß's cross into his own net and Brighton have brought it back to 3-2 👀 pic.twitter.com/maBMwVu3DC

Gomez has already missed two chances in this second half and he now has his third opportunity since the break. His powerful effort from the right side of the box forces Martinez into a decent save at his near post...

England head coach Thomas Tuchel is at Stamford Bridge today. He won’t have like Cole Palmer’s miss much and Palmer is probably the only Chelsea attacking player not to have impressed so far. There’s still time, though.

Chelsea have two big chances to score a fourth but cannot take either. First, Neto takes advantage of poor defending from Kadioglu and has a shot saved at the near post by Verbruggen. Then Palmer has a glorious opportunity inside the six-yard box from Rogers’ cross but somehow Palmer guides it over the bar. I am going to say it now that I do not think we have seen an end to the goals today.

Fofana is rightly booked for an earlier challenge on De Cuyper as he completely took him out and Brighton now have a free-kick deep into the Chelsea half after a foul by Neto.

Boscagli clips a lovely free-kick to the back post, where he perfectly picks out Gomez, who has a free header from the edge of the six-yard box but his powerful header goes wide of the far post. That should have been a goal and that is a mighty let-off for Chelsea.

Gomez has a decent chance for Brighton on the edge of the Chelsea penalty area but he fires his effort well wide.

Chelsea attack from back to front, with Martinez launching a long ball forward from inside his own box to pick out the run of Pedro into the Brighton half. Pedro ends up having a shot blocked inside the Brighton penalty area.

Palmer was very influential for Chelsea at Fulham on Monday night and, despite Chelsea scoring three first-half goals, he has been quiet today.

We are back under way at Stamford Bridge. Despite Chelsea being two goals ahead, it does not feel like Brighton are out of this one.

Chelsea 3 Brighton 1Leeds 0 Brentford 1Sunderland 0 Fulham 0

Possession: Chelsea 29%-71% BrightonShots: 9-6Shots on target: 4-3Corners: 2-4Touches in opposition box: 15-10

Chelsea go in 3-1 at half-time, having only had 29.3 per cent of possession. They finished with about 35 per cent possession in the 3-2 victory over Fulham, so it seems Alonso is setting his team up very much as a counter-attacking side. It’s all very Antonio Conte.

Vuskovic has a late effort in the first half from range and it goes just over Martinez’s bar.

The first half is then brought to an end not long after and Chelsea take a 3-1 lead into the break.

The Brighton fans enjoy an audacious Pedro backheel that does not come off. Moments later, Gross clips in a cross from the right that picks out Gomez in the box but his header goes over the bar.

There will be two added minutes at the end of this first half.

There has been a goal in one of the other 2pm kick-offs. At Elland Road, Brentford, who were one of the most impressive teams on the opening weekend, have taken the lead over Leeds through Schade.

After a dreadful clearance from Dunk, Rogers shoots from just outside the box but it goes wide of Verbruggen’s left post.

Pedro has a shot blocked inside the Brighton area before Rogers also has an effort blocked.

At 3-0 down, they looked down and out but maybe the visitors have a route back into the game. Kostoulas is denied by Martinez before the ball comes to Yalcouye, who volleys first time. His emphatic effort smashes off the inside of the far post and into the net. A fine way to score your first Premier League goal and maybe this game is not over quite yet.

"Yalcouye with a sumptuous volley!"Malick Yalcouye puts Brighton on the scoreboard with a venomous volley 😳 pic.twitter.com/8UeeyvPjUw

There have already been three goals in the first half at Stamford Bridge but it is still goalless at Elland Road and the Stadium of Light in the other two 2pm kick-offs.

The Brighton fans have been singing ‘The Falklands are ours’ at Chelsea’s Argentine substitute Valentin Barco. Barco was part of the Argentina squad who celebrated his nation’s World Cup win over England by displaying a Falklands banner. The Brighton fans had also been giving the club’s former striker Joao Pedro some stick. Pedro celebrated his goal right in front of them. Touche.

The Brazilian missed a sitter earlier but he makes no mistake this time and goes to celebrate in front of the travelling Brighton fans. Pedro owes a lot of gratitude from Hato, who drives down Chelsea’s left from inside his own half to the edge of the Brighton box. The Dutchman passes to his left to find Pedro, who takes one touch before clinically slotting home into the far corner. Is that game, set and match?

Joao Pedro finishes off a deadly Chelsea counter-attack and gives the Blues a 3-0 lead 🔥 pic.twitter.com/wAr0ckIgXJ

Brighton have their first real sighter on goal. Gomez clips in a lovely delivery to the far post to pick out the run of Yalcouye into the box. Yalcouye gets to it on the stretch and his effort is straight at Martinez.

Brighton have had 70% possession but their xG currently sits at 0.03. Despite having a lot of the ball, they really have not looked like scoring. You do though have to bear in mind that they are without forwards like Minteh, Rutter and Mitoma due to injury. Will Minteh still be a Brighton player when the window shuts?

How has Pedro missed? The former Brighton man absolutely should have put Chelsea 3-0 up and that could have been game, set and match. The ball is played in behind down the right channel and Neto outmuscles Kadioglu, who goes to ground near the byline. Neto then unselfishly from the right side of the box squares it for Pedro, who takes a few touches before getting his shot away. It seems harder to miss than to score but somehow puts his effort wide of the far post.

After Martinez easily catches a corner from Gross, the Chelsea fans start singing the name of their new goalkeeper.

Brighton are dominating posession but are yet to have a shot. Chelsea meanwhile have had three shots, all on target, and have scored twice.

The hosts have their second inside the opening quarter of an hour. Rogers does well on the left side of the box to hold off Vuskovic before squaring the ball. Neto runs across Kadioglu’s blindside and pokes home first time from eight yards out. Kadioglu should really have dealt with that and was too flat-footed. He should not have allowed Neto to get to that ball first.

"Pedro Neto Pounces!"Morgan Rogers goes past his defender before sliding the ball across to Neto! 💥 pic.twitter.com/WHZCIGsOLl

The travelling Brighton fans are making sure that Pedro knows what they think of their former player.

Up in the stands, England boss Thomas Tuchel is sat next to Brazil manager Carlo Ancelotti, both former Chelsea bosses.

Since the start of the 2024/25 season, no goalkeeper in the Premier League has made more errors leading to goals than Verbruggen’s 10. Second on that list; Sanchez, who is not in the Chelsea squad today.

Brighton win their first corner of the afternoon and Martinez is forced into action, punching away at his near post as the delivery threatened to creep in.

That is an absolute gift for the home side after a huge error from Brighton. Pedro flicks on at the near post and Wieffer makes the block near his own line. Verbruggen then tries to catch the loose ball but he and Wieffer end up getting into each others’ way. The ball then falls to Lavia, who pokes home. As they did at Craven Cottage the other night, Chelsea hit the front early.

"It's a nightmare for the goalkeeper!"Bart Verbruggen and Mats Wieffer's collision leads to Romeo Lavia scoring his first goal for Chelsea ⚽️ pic.twitter.com/q5awbdwVV0

There was a fist pump from Chelsea’s new set-piece coach Austin MacPhee after Romeo Lavia’s goal from the corner. It looks like MacPhee will be claiming credit for that one, even though it came thanks to an error from Brighton goalkeeper Bart Verbruggen. Xabi Alonso also celebrated with MacPhee.

Chelsea win the first corner of the afternoon after Dunk blocked Neto’s cross...

He might be trying to sell his shares in Chelsea, but co-owner Todd Boehly is at today’s game in the Stamford Bridge stands.

Before we get going, Stamford Bridge pays tribute to Bobby Tambling and Ken Bates, who both died over the summer. Wreaths are laid in their memory with their families carrying framed pictures of the two men.

Both sides emerge from the tunnel at Stamford Bridge and we are moments away from kick-off in west London. Here is a reminder of how the two sides line up this afternoon:

As you’d expect, there were big cheers for Emi Martinez from the Chelsea fans ahead of kick-off. He responded by shaking a fist in the air and giving them a big round of applause. This is his first game since the World Cup final for Argentina.

Chelsea had gone 77 League games without fielding a player aged 30 plus before handing goalkeeper Emi Martinez a debut today. The Argentine celebrates his 34th birthday on September 2. The last played aged 30-plus to appear for the club was Thiago Silva, who was 39 at the time.

“We are delighted to have him. To have a goalkeeper of his stature, his personality, I think he will bring a lot of qualities. I am sure he can have a straight impact. We spoke, he felt ready to play, so here we go.”

“We will see. It was a decision we thought was good for the team, for the club. Sometimes you have to take tough decisions because this one is an important one. But now we need to look forward.”

On Enzo Fernandez being left out of the matchday squad:

“We assess what is best for the team and considering everything, the situation, we need a team that is focused, with everyone involved that is fully committed and engaged with the game.”

Emiliano Martínez turns 34 on September 2 and by most tangible metrics, the goalkeeper is past his peak.

But it is the intangibles that set Martínez apart and why his availability at a knock-down price from Aston Villa convinced Chelsea to seize a market opportunity.

At £7.5m, Martínez could prove to be Chelsea’s smartest piece of business of the summer and there is little doubt he will be box-office at Stamford Bridge.

“I am delighted to be at this football club,” Martinez said. “Coming to Chelsea, for me and my family, was an easy decision to make and I am just over the moon; I cannot wait to get started.

“I want to be successful here. I am someone who wants to win at everything I do and I want to bring that here to this football club because it is a football club that wins titles, so I think it is a good match. I am all passion and I play with my heart. I will give 100 per cent every game, every training session to make the club, my teammates and the supporters proud.”

Xabi Alonso takes charge of his first home Premier League game in charge of Chelsea as they host Brighton at Stamford Bridge. Both sides were in action in two different competitions on Thursday night. Chelsea reached the League Cup third round as they beat Luton 2-0 at Stamford Bridge, with former Brighton man Danny Welbeck scoring on his debut. Brighton meanwhile confirmed their place in the Conference League group stages with a 4-0 aggregate win over Tromso.

Chelsea began their Premier League campaign last Monday in a west London derby against Fulham at Craven Cottage, winning 3-2 in Alonso’s first game as Chelsea boss. Enzo Fernandez was not involved in Chelsea’s squad against Luton on Thursday and has been heavily linked with a move to Manchester City. Alonso was asked about Enzo’s absence on Thursday and did not confirm whether the Argentine would be involved today.

“It was just because of the game today [on Thursday] and we have other players who need minutes,” Alonso said. “[On Wednesday], in the afternoon. It is a decision that I took. Enzo is a good professional. He is training well and I have nothing to say about this. It was just decisions that we have to take thinking about the game that we were playing tonight [Thursday]. We will see for Sunday [today].”

Brighton began their Premier League campaign in emphatic style as they thrashed Aston Villa 4-0 at home seven days ago. Jack Hinshelwood scored twice in that game but will now miss a number of weeks with an ankle injury. They are also without Yankuba Minteh, who has been linked with a move to Liverpool this summer but is unavailable due to injury.

“When the window is closed I demand from him [Minteh] that he is fully committed to this club,” Brighton boss Fabian Hurzeler said. “There are dreams and wishes for players, but in the end we always need to figure out what is best for the club.

“We have had an exchange with him. At the moment he is definitely a Brighton player. It is very important to understand his thoughts but also our planning. As a club we try to develop players. The last few years have shown that the whole environment gave him a lot of trust and belief that he is capable of having this progress. It is always a give and take and he has gotten a lot from us.”

Brighton won both Premier League meetings last season, winning 3-1 in this fixture last September. Brighton have won five of their last eight top-flight meetings with Chelsea. Team news from Stamford Bridge to follow shortly.

Newcastle United players who are part of the solution

Lukas Hornicek, Lewis Hall, Amar Dedic, Malick Thiaw, Dan Burn, Lewis Miley, Sean Steur, Fabian Schar (as a back up for rest of season)

Newcastle United players where it is unfair/impossible to judge as not seen enough of them

William Osula (he has still only started 12 Premier League matches for NUFC), Aladji Bamba (0 PL starts), Nico Gonzalez (8 EPL starts for NUFC), Ewen Jaouen (0 PL starts), Bazoumana Toure (0 EPL starts), Matias Fernandez-Pardo (4 EPL starts)

Newcastle United players who are part of the problem (and can they be part of the solution (marked Yes, No, Maybe?)

Tino Livramento – Yes. We know he is a quality player BUT can he ever stay fit?

Sven Botman – Maybe. Was absolutely brilliant in his first (2022-23) season when United had best defence in the Premier League. Two big operations/injuries and hasn’t been able to get back to that level on a consistent basis. So far.

Joelinton – No. May seem a bit harsh but he is another who has been heavily impacted by injuries, plus he is now into his 30s. I think as well that if Newcastle are to play a mobile passing game, our “Only cost forty million” Brazilian doesn’t fit in.

Jacob Ramsey – Maybe.  Has shown at times he has the quality but not able to put a run of form together of any length as a starter, injuries not helping. I think by the end of this season we will know either way. With United losing the likes of Tonali and Bruno, Ramsey should be making a starting eleven position his own.

Joe Willock – No. He was brilliant in the 2022-23 then had really bad time with injuries. We have seen at times the necessary quality and impact this season in glimpses but he isn’t able to do enough to be a certain starter.

Harvey Barnes – Maybe. Always the issue with Harvey, if he can get into goalscoring positions he is Newcastle’s best finisher. When he doesn’t though, his overall contribution is rarely enough to deserve a starting place. Last season Barnes started 19 Premier League matches and came off the bench in 18 of the other 19. It feels very much like he represents the team/squad going backwards as he starts week in week out now. I do like him but can he show enough to be more than a supersub?

Anthony Elanga – Maybe. Started the season on fire AND looking a real goal threat. Unlucky to then pick up an injury in training. I think it is possible he can prove his doubters wrong but a case of hope for the best but fear the worst.

Jacob Murphy – No. A bit like Willock and into his 30s now. His standout season of 2024-25 in now history. Has produced a few quality moments this season but doesn’t produce enough over whole matches to be a starter.

Yoane Wissa – Maybe. Very much like Elanga, a case of hope for the best but fear the worst.

When I talk about those who I have listed as part of the solution, it isn’t necessarily that I see them as world beaters, more a case of I think they are definitely good enough to at least perform at a certain level which we now need.

Obviously there weren’t many of them that I could list and Schar is only as back up for this season, whilst with Dan Burn he turns 35 in May and so realistically, he could hopefully do another full season in 2027-28.

What we clearly need is for some of those who in the ‘impossible to judge yet’ to come through and prove themselves as time goes on.

Whilst more immediately, we really need some of those in the ‘part of the problem’ list above, to prove themselves real assets very soon AND prove the doubters wrong!

#1968. Scott Parker Reunion Could Be Key to West Ham Defensive Deal

No sooner had Scott Parker been appointed as West Ham’s ‘promotion specialist’ manager than stories surfaced linking him with the recruitment of former players.

Reports linking West Ham with C J Egan-Riley are unlikely to disappear anytime soon, with the former Burnley defender continuing to attract attention following his rapid development this season.

Egan-Riley enjoyed a breakthrough campaign previously under Scott Parker, establishing himself as one of the Championship’s standout young defenders and helping Burnley secure promotion back to the Premier League.

A move to the London Stadium would carry several attractions. Not only does Parker know the player well from their time together at Burnley, but Egan-Riley would also qualify as a home-grown player, an increasingly valuable asset for West Ham who are looking to balance squad registration requirements.

Parker has consistently praised the defender in the past, and stated he was a key player for him in the Championship. He was instrumental in the defender’s development, giving him a prominent role in Burnley’s promotion-winning side. His composure on the ball, ability to play across the back line and potential for further improvement make him the type of profile West Ham are expected to target.

Defensive stalwart for Scott Parker’s West Ham?

The central defender chose Marseille ahead of West Ham in 2025, who secured his signature on a free transfer after the expiry of his Burnley contract, meaning any transfer fee received would represent a substantial profit on their investment.

Having been a bit part player at the French club in his first season, following a squad overhaul in the summer he is now a regular starter and the data shows he has maintained a 93% pass completion in Ligue 1. The 23 year old ranks as one of the leagues most accurate passers in his position.

There is also reason to believe Marseille would be willing sellers. The French giants have made no secret of the fact that they will need to generate funds through player departures during the January transfer window due to ongoing financial issues. West Ham have enjoyed a productive relationship with Marseille over the years, with deals for Dimitri Payet, Emerson and Nayef Aguerd demonstrating that negotiations between the two clubs are far from uncommon.

The structure of any potential deal, be it an initial loan or a straight transfer, is yet to emerge. Either way, if the Hammers can persuade the defender to play a part in their quest for promotion they would be adding a young, home-grown centre-back who appears far from reaching his full potential.

I have been a season ticket holder since the late eighties, so experienced the highs and lows of being a West Ham supporter. I previously wrote for OLAS and have contributed to a number of football publications in the past.

#1967. ‘Right now…’ – Liverpool-linked Premier League star makes his plans clear amid transfer rumours

One Premier League player who’s reportedly being targeted by Liverpool has issued a reponse to the transfer speculation surrounding him.

Earlier this week, TEAMtalk claimed that Anfield chiefs are eyeing Bart Verbruggen as a potential long-term successor to Alisson Becker, who’s now 34 and – as it stands – will be out of contract in seven months’ time.

The Brighton goalkeeper was reportedly among a shortlist of candidates being considered by the Reds prior to the summer transfer window, with the Merseysiders eventually agreeing a deal to sign Lucca Brughmans, who’ll join from Genk next summer.

Verbruggen – who’s currently with the Netherlands squad for their concluding UEFA Nations League fixtures – has insisted that despite the rumoured interest from Liverpool, he’s more than happy with the Seagulls, who currently sit second in the Premier League.

The 24-year-old said (via NOS): “Right now we’re doing really well at Brighton, so it would be a real shame to ruin that by living in the future. I really try to stay in the moment, to focus on what is currently going on. I enjoy that, and that is also how I perform best.”

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

Brighton’s magnificent season so far has been underpinned by the excellence of the man between the sticks, who’s kept seven clean sheets in 10 league games and conceded just three times in eight top-flight matches since a 4-3 defeat at Chelsea in August (Transfermarkt).

Figures from Fotmob show that he’s prevented 4.39 xG worth of goals for his team, more than anyone else in the Premier League, and he put in a heroic display in the Seagulls’ recent win at Manchester City as he recorded no fewer than seven saves (Sky Sports).

Those performance levels would indicate that he’d be an ideal successor to Alisson, although there’s been renewed hope in recent days that Liverpool’s number 1 could extend his contract for another year or two, with his agent currently in talks with the club to that effect.

Giorgi Mamardashvili was signed with the intention of succeeding the Brazilian eventually, although the 26-year-old hasn’t always convinced during his time with the Reds so far, and Brughmans will add to the queue once he joins ahead of next season.

Right now there wouldn’t seem to be any urgent need for LFC to move heaven and earth to sign Verbruggen, but if circumstances were to change regarding their current goalkeeping options, it could be worth keeping a hand in should the opportunity arise to move for the Brighton stopper.

#1966. “Cashing in” on Castellanos claim ignores one major stumbling block | West Ham News

Ever since the closing days of the summer transfer window there have been claims that West Ham will be cashing in on Taty Castellanos in the winter: The Argentine has been a huge disappointment in the 15 games of West Ham’s championship season, with just a solitary goal to show for his efforts.

At times he’s resembled more of a moody, disinterested bystander and seems pretty much the most likely player in the eleven to be yellow carded each time he plays.

A solitary goal is plain unacceptable for the frontman who cost £27 million: Claims that he’ll be sold in the winter abound.

Sadly, Everton’s late interest in the summer window, reportedly around £40 million, appears to have evaporated as Taty’s form has waned. Understandably.

Far from happy: One goal in fifteen means Castellanos has been a huge let down in the second tier. Its also means those big money suitors have now evaporated

The newest suggestions from EFL specialist site the72.co.uk suggest Castellanos could be heading back home – however there’s a catch:

“River Plate reportedly view the 28-year-old as a priority target in their striker search, although the finances involved in the deal could prove to be a major hurdle. However, cashing in could give WHUFC the chance to sign a true talisman to aid their promotion bid. “

“Cashing in”? I think not: That’s the elephant in the room here. River Plate have already disclosed that they’ll look at some kind of loan or shared purchase option – as they’re short of funds – which of course will cut no ice with West Ham who will want to replace Taty with a striker more suited to scoring the Championship goals they require.

Merely shipping Taty out on loan without a permanent sale will serve no useful purpose and could actually weaken Scott Parker’s squad. The Hammers have enough loaned – out unwanted stars as it is: Another one added to the list won’t help a rebuild. The only possible route could involve a swap for goal keeper Santiago Beltran – which would still leave the Hammers short of a goal scorer and needing to offload Hermansen or Areola in the winter.

And how often to these player swaps ever come off? Exactly.

#1964. GdS: Milan ready €50m January assault for Tresoldi to give Ramos a partner – the strategy

AC Milan are serious about signing Nicolo Tresoldi from Club Brugge, with an attempt being readied ahead of the winter window.

According to La Gazzetta dello Sport, Milan intend to sign another striker even before the summer arrives, in order to boost their Champions League hopes. The name that they have chosen is someone the fans already know well: Nicolo Tresoldi.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

At the end of June, the club announced the signing of Gonçalo Ramos for over €70m, the most expensive signing in the club’s history to date (and likely for a while to come). Ramos hasn’t – at least for now – cured Milan’s goal-scoring deficiency in the No.9 role.

The negotiations for Tresoldi, however, are shaping up to be costly. Last summer, Club Brugge rejected another Italian offer of €35m from Roma, and in the meantime the price has skyrocketed after the forward bagged 13 goals in 15 games.

Adding his four goals this season against Germany’s youth team brings him close to 20 for the season already. His league hat-trick against VV Sint-Truiden at the end of October followed his hat-trick at San Siro against Inter, marking the night that every Rossoneri fan knew his name.

Therefore, the cost could now be around €50m, another huge expense if Milan really decide to go all-in. The club made a €24m loss in the last accounts after three years of profit, and the temptation is to speculate to accumulate, i.e. to invest more and make sure of the Champions League revenues.

There’s a desire to finalise the deal as early as the January transfer window, unless Brugge move to raise the price, perhaps due to a potential foreign competition. Milan believe that their relationship with the Belgian side is actually strong, with Gerry Cardinale ready to lead talks again.

As for Ramos, the investment so far has yielded just three goals and two assists, which doesn’t mean he wasn’t effective and is ready to be shelved, but it’s precisely when paired with another striker that the management believes the Portuguese could be more productive.

In short, a two-striker team can’t be ruled out in the future, with Tresoldi alongside the former Benfica man. In the European race goals fuel the climb, and Milan know this after last season’s late collapse, keen to avoid it again.

Should Milan hit a wall erected by Club Brugge, they would leave the Tresoldi option open for the summer. In the meantime, they would fill the gap with a striker on loan from a top European club.

However, Tresoldi could provide an initial assist for Milan: his support for the Rossoneri is well-known and has been publicly stated, so among the various options available, Nicolò would choose the San Siro.

A permanent return to Italy could also benefit coach Roberto Mancini, who – after the Under-21 European Championship (which Tresoldi will compete in with Germany) – would finally like him to play for the senior Azzurri side.

Nicolò, born in Cagliari in August 2004, is still free to choose which (senior) national team he wants to represent, and Mancini expressed his confidence earlier this week: “I spoke to Tresoldi, and Ranieri spoke to us too. First of all, I think he needs to feel the desire to play for Italy.

“He was born in Italy, like his father [former defender Emanuele], who played for the Under-21s and won the European Championship. I think there’s a chance he’ll choose the Azzurri. He knows he can be an important player for our future, and I hope he makes the right choice.”

#1961. The one key question on which nearly all West Ham fans are in agreement

It is not often that West Ham fans appear unified over anything, after recent seasons of strife, division, disagreement and dispute with the Sullivan and Brady leadership, it feels as if ‘disharmony’ has been the default setting.

Not, it seems, about everything. There is one hot topic on which a huge majority of West Ham fans are in almost total agreement.

According to the NY Times’ fan survey, the biggest consensus was not for the approval of the new manager – although there is a pretty strong 77% majority of fans who responded who give the appointment of Scott Parker the thumbs up.

The biggest single factor on which most West Ham supporters agree is the choice of goalkeeper. According to the survey:

“Of the fans surveyed, an overwhelming 85.4 per cent believe Alphonse Areola should reclaim the No 1 jersey from Mads Hermansen.

Likeable yes, dependable no: 85% of West Ham fans want Hermansen out of the team

Interestingly, though, a sizeable 62 per cent of supporters believe the travelling contingent at Ewood Park were not right to boo Hermansen.”

Eighty five percent of fans have had enough of the Dane’s inept performances in between the sticks, with one fan driven to comment that West Ham’s goal would be better defended simply by hanging a green jersey on the cross bar rather than continuing to select the out of form Hermansen.

Of course the fly in the ointment is that Areola has been reported as ‘unfit’ – whether that means third choice Finlay Herrick comes into consideration – who can say- but it’d be a brave selection for Parker to leave his number one on the bench if Areola isn’t ready for the Preston North End fixture next weekend, however much it seems supporters want to see Hermansen out of the team.

#1960. Joe Hart pinpoints ‘unbelievable’ Alisson Becker trait which makes him ‘one of the best’

Joe Hart has proclaimed that Alisson Becker will ‘forever be regarded as one of the best’ goalkeepers to have graced the Premier League.

Liverpool’s number 1 has been rightly acknowledged as one of the foremost players in his position in world football since his move to Anfield in 2018 and has been pivotal towards the trophies won by the Reds in that time.

He produced one of his greatest LFC performances in the victory at Crystal Palace last weekend, with his tally of six saves including a world-class reaction stop from Daichi Kamada which left the Eagles attacker astounded.

In an interview with The Athletic, Hart lavished praise on Alisson for the consistency he’s shown throughout his time in England, and especially his prowess in one-on-saves.

The ex-Manchester City stopper said of the 34-year-old: “One of the best to do it in the Premier League. What I love is his simplicity. He’s not necessarily eye-catching in the way he moves, but it’s the way he deals with everything.

“He makes massive saves. His one-on-one technique is unbelievable, and he has made it his own. He very rarely gets beaten one-on-one, which in this Premier League is incredible because you’re up against some of the best strikers in the world.

“He’s struggled a bit with injuries lately, but I think he’ll forever be regarded as one of the best to play the position.”

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

Last weekend, Alisson produced a perfect example of the one-on-one ability that Hart pinpointed by thwarting Yeremy Pino when the Crystal Palace forward was through on goal, a significant intervention at a time that Liverpool were 2-0 up.

When it comes to ‘massive saves’, it mightn’t quite be in the same category as his legendary stoppage-time heroics against Napoli in December 2018 when our Champions League campaign was in the balance, but it showed that the 34-year-old remains a world-class goalkeeper.

His outstanding display at Selhurst Park came after a couple of costly misjudgements in defeats to Arsenal and Fenerbahce, which shows the Brazilian’s strength of character to put those unfortunate moments behind him and come up trumps for his team.

Alisson’s agent Ze Maria revealed in recent days that talks have begun over a prospective contract renewal at Liverpool, with the Reds’ number 1 having said after the win at Palace that he’d like to stay at Anfield beyond the expiry of his current deal next summer.

More heroics like those he produced in south London four days ago, and an extension to his existing terms should be a no-brainer for sporting director Julian Ward.

#1959. Rising Newcastle United stars experience harsh Swedish lessons with the Young Lions

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

The Young Lions had a thrilling 3-2 victory against the Netherlands on Wednesday.

However, a different story when the England Under 18s ran into Sweden this weekend in their second of three matches in Valencia.

Rising Newcastle United stars Roman Dowell and Kyran Thompson started against Sweden.

An attacking player, Kyran Thompson recently turned 17 and has been in brilliant form for the Newcastle United Under 18s and Under 21s so far this season. He decided to leave Arsenal and join Newcastle this summer gone.

Whilst 16-year-old Newcastle United goalkeeper Roman Dowell (pictured at the top of this report) is making great strides at NUFC. Like Kyran Thompson, Dowell has also been in great form for both the Newcastle United Under 18s and Under 21s this season.

At the Oliva Nova venue in Valencia the Young Lions given some harsh Swedish lessons.

There were no real signs of what was to come in a pretty even uneventful opening half.

However, the Young Lions swiftly found themselves 2-0 down in no time after the break.

Roman Dowell left badly exposed by those in front of him, with Leonel Eklund scoring shortly after the restart and then Marlon Ebietomere made it 2-0 only minutes later.

Then with 17 minutes to go it was more of the same, Sweden going 3-0 when Eklund grabbed his second goal.

Roman Dowell played the full match, whilst his NUFC teammate Kyran Thompson was taken off just before the hour mark.

Some tough lessons to be learnt and for the United pair and their England teammates, at this early stage of their careers sometimes you learn more from a defeat such as this one than you do when you are winning.

Final score: Sweden Under 18s 3 England Under 18s 0

England: 13 Roman Dowell (Newcastle United), 3 Calvin Diakite (Chelsea), 5 Marlow Barrett (Manchester City), 6 Tyrese Noubissie (RC Strasbourg), 7 Ryan Kavuma-McQueen (Portsmouth, loan from Chelsea), 8 Hugo De Lisle (Leicester City), 12 Riley Ebho (Chelsea), 14 Kyran Thompson (Newcastle United), 16 Reon Smith (West Ham United), 17 Oliver Boast (Tottenham Hotspur), 20 Erik Farkas (Liverpool).

Substitutes: 23 Jacob Watson (Manchester United) for Diakite 24’, 11 Jeremy Monga (Swansea City, loan from Manchester City) for Kavuma-McQueen 46’, 18 Max Little (Southampton) for De Lisle 46’, 21 Jerome Abbey (Wolverhampton Wanderers) for Noubissie 59’, 9 Jashayde Greenwood (Chelsea) for Thompson 59’, 10 Samuel Alker (Leeds United) for Farkas 59, 15 Gabriel Sambou (Chelsea) for Ebho 71’, 19 Teddie Lamb (Manchester City) for Boast 71’

It is Switzerland v England kick-off 3pm GMT, Monday 16 November, to finish off this trio of Young Lions matches in Valencia.

The 6’5 Czech powerhouse was involved in international duty last week as Spain ran out 2 – 0 victors over his national side.

However there’s a development today that would suggest Koppen needs a plan B: The striker’s own thoughts on leaving Scotland are revealed in Thehardtackle.com’s article this afternoon:

The 23-year-old has become an important part of Derek McInnes’ plans this season, producing nine goals and six assists in 17 appearances. His form has inevitably attracted attention, with West Ham among the clubs considering him as they look to strengthen their attack.

However, Naderi is understood to be happy at Ibrox and does not see a move to the London Stadium as an attractive proposition while West Ham remain in the second tier.”

Without their Premier League status to attract new recruits  and current languishing in ninth place  in the Championship, you’d sense West Ham have a very difficult transfer window ahead if they cannot climb back up towards the automatic promotion slots ahead of the window opening in January.

Koppen will not only need a plan B but quite possibly a C, D,E F and G.
